thread.title: Have You Heard The One About USA Today, Lifeguards And FANG Stocks? | Seeking Alpha

author: The Heisenberg
title: Have You Heard The One About USA Today, Lifeguards And FANG Stocks? | Seeking Alpha
text:
On Thursday, USA Today published an article advising teenagers and college kids to plow their summer job money into Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Netflix ( NFLX ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ). Just read this quote from that piece:
A $10-per-hour summer job slinging eggs or saving lives at the beach [is] enough seed money to build a small fortune in a short period of time ... in four FANG stocks.
When my Twitter feed starting lighting up with jokes about that article on Friday morning, I was posted up in a yellow lawn chair not 50 yards away from an actual lifeguard (if you're a Heisenberg newcomer, I live on an island so there are a lot of anecdotes to that effect in my writing).
I looked down the beach at the guy sitting under one of those iconic red umbrellas and considered him in light of the above linked article. I couldn't help but think of the famous picture that made the rounds back in 2015 during the Chinese equity bubble when, apparently, at least one local banana vendor decided to take up trading as a side hustle:
To be clear, there are a number of great arguments you can make on the way to contending that big cap tech ( QQQ ) isn't a bubble. Goldman published an expansive note to that effect this week and while I didn't find it wholly convincing, they offered up a characteristically trenchant argument for why "this time may be different" (so to speak) when it comes to sectoral dominance of the equity market. For example, "dominance" doesn't mean what it used to and thus might fairly be described as less concerning now than it was decades ago:
(Goldman)
That said, it is clearly ridiculous to suggest, as USA Today does, that "teens and college-age workers" should put whatever meager wages they can earn from "slinging eggs" in June and July into just four stocks which, according to the May installment of BofAML's Global Fund Manager survey, constitute the most crowded trade on the planet.
Besides advising lifeguards to pile into a notoriously crowded trade, there are myriad other issues with USA Today's "recommendation", not the least of which is the fact that USA Today is making stock recommendations in the first place. Suffice to say I had quite a bit of fun lampooning that article in a post for Dealbreaker out Friday morning.
But jokes aside (and I'm having a really hard time restraining myself from making the same jokes here that I made in that Dealbreaker piece), people are still funneling money into tech in a big way. Here's Bloomberg's Andrew Cinko:
The money flowing into technology is becoming seriously large. BofAML strategists report the $2.3 billion that went into tech funds in the latest week was the second-largest ever, putting the sector on pace for its biggest annual inflow on record (based on EPFR data). The burgeoning risk, says BofA, is that when trouble hits, investors have to sell what they own, and more and more ownership is being concentrated in tech.
Here's the chart from the actual BofAML note that Cinko cites:
(BofAML)
Again, this doesn't have to spell trouble, but it is worth noting that the rally in tech is showing signs of being ever more dependent on the same handful of names that USA Today (and probably a lot of your favorite mainstream pundits) are telling lifeguards to buy. In fact, as of Monday, every FANG stock was in overbought territory:
(Bloomberg)
As Bloomberg's Luke Kawa wrote earlier this week , "the last time each member of FANG had a 14-day RSI [above 70] was January 25, 2017."
In the same post, Kawa also notes that the FANG index is trading at a record relative to the "broader" (and the scare quotes are there for obvious reasons), Nasdaq 100 ( QQQ ). Here's the chart on that, which is annotated to show you the stretch in late March when a combination of regulatory concerns and the President's harsh words for Amazon triggered a fleeting rout in the tech space:
(Heisenberg)
The problem here is the same as it ever was. I don't want to get back into the Howard Marks " perpetual motion machine " argument again, but the bottom line is that this is a self-fulfilling prophecy that's turbocharged by passive investing and the proliferation of these names across multiple factor-based products. I tied all of this together recently in a fairly lengthy post on smart-beta.
The more ubiquitous these high fliers become, the more inflows they receive and that serves to drive them inexorably higher. Because they are so dominate at the index level, their performance in turn drives benchmarks up and that forces hedge funds and other active managers to dive into them too in order to avoid underperformance. Consider this from the latest installment of Goldman's hedge fund monitor:
Funds maintain conviction in their top positions. Hedge fund portfolio turnover remained near record lows during the volatile 1Q. The average fund carries 68% of its long portfolio in its top 10 positions, nearly an all-time high. Nine of the top 10 stocks in our VIP list last quarter remain in the top 10 this quarter. FB, which ranked as #2 last quarter, experienced the largest net increase in popularity among all stocks during 1Q. AAPL, AMZN, GOOGL, and NFLX ranked among the stocks with the largest decreases in popularity, but remain near the top of the VIP list.
See what I mean? As BofAML writes in the note cited above, the more ownership gets concentrated in these names, the more likely it is they'll be sold to raise cash when something or other comes along and destabilizes markets.
You can only sell what you own and if everyone owns the same names, well then that's what gets sold.
Take a look at this chart:
(Heisenberg)
There have been two panic bids for Treasurys ( TLT ) over the past two days, one on Thursday when the Brazilian real was crashing towards 4.00 and another at 4:00 in the morning (New York time) on Friday. As you can see from the annotation in the chart above, the Friday safe haven bid was catalyzed by a Nikkei story about Apple informing its supply chain to get ready for around 20% fewer components for iPhones hitting the market in the latter half of 2018.
That Apple headline and the flight to safety it catalyzed early Friday morning while U.S. traders were still asleep was followed by a big block trade at 9:18 London time (24,116 TYU8 futures blocked 119-27+; $1.8m/dv01; equating to $2.1b of current 10-year bonds). Here's what S&P ( SPY ) futures did at the same time:
(Heisenberg)
Now consider all of that with this visual:
(Goldman)
As Pee-wee Herman would say: " connect the dots, la, la, la ".
For investors in general, the overarching point here is that the market is highly dependent on these names and the setup described above and detailed extensively by Howard Marks last summer suggests that dependence will probably grow over time. The more influential they are, the more likely it is that any weakness in those names will spill over into other assets, potentially causing a domino effect.
For instance, when algos see something like those panic bids for Treasurys shown above, they're likely to chase down the rabbit hole, potentially exaggerating the move or worse, pull back altogether on the assumption that something is going on that they, by virtue of being algos and not humans, aren't capable of understanding. That latter point sounds funny, but lest you should think I'm just making it up, do note that it's a real phenomenon. You can read more than you would ever care to know about HFTs and "adverse selection" here .
Coming full circle to USA Today and the relative wisdom of advising the lifeguard crowd to invest their summer job money in FANG stocks, there is no question as to whether these are fantastic businesses with the potential to expand their global reach and generally become even more dominate over time. But they are an exceptionally crowded trade and it is entirely unreasonable to assume that inexperienced would-be investors know the first thing about all of the points laid out above.
And even if those folks were inclined to familiarize themselves with the prevailing dynamics in FANG, it still wouldn't be a good idea to put all your eggs in one basket (and according to USA Today, college kids are "slinging eggs" during the summer, so I guess "eggs in one basket" can be taken both figuratively and literally here). That is, if you were making your first investment in equities, you wouldn't want to eschew a broad-based S&P index fund for four tech stocks, especially considering the fact that an investment in a broad-based index fund will by definition give you some exposure to those same names anyway.
One day, we may all look back on USA Today's lifeguard article as evidence that they do indeed ring bells at the top.
Until then, I guess I'm going to need to walk up and down the beach and implore the college crowd to ignore USA Today.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
